whyThisMatters: A lot of what feels true about security is old advice or only half right. A few minutes here will clear up the common myths, so you can protect yourself and your team with confidence.
rememberThis: Old security advice can be wrong. If a rule sounds too easy or too comfortable ("I'm too small to target", "the padlock means safe"), check it again before you trust it.

discussionPrompts: Ask who has heard "nobody would want my data" at work. What could an attacker actually do with one ordinary email account?
Ask the group which myth they believed until today. Where did they first hear it?
For the MFA and antivirus myths, ask: what is one extra layer you already use (a phone prompt, a lock on your screen) and what would happen if it failed?
Ask honestly: would you report something you were not sure about? What would make it easier?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get mf-05 wrong. "Strong password" sounds like a lifelong safe state, so many say TRUE. It is false: a strong password that appears in a data breach is already known to attackers and must be changed straight away.

items.myth: I have nothing worth stealing, so attackers will not bother with me.
items.fact: Attackers target everyone. Your account, your contacts and your access to work systems are all valuable, even if you feel ordinary.
items.detail: Criminals mostly use automated tools that send millions of messages and see who answers. A hacked email account can be used to scam your colleagues, reset other passwords or reach company files. You are often the easiest way in, not the final target.

items.myth: Antivirus software alone keeps me fully protected.
items.fact: Antivirus is one useful layer, not a complete shield. It cannot stop you from handing over a password or approving a fake request.
items.detail: Antivirus mainly spots known bad files. It cannot tell if an email is a scam or if a caller is lying. Keep it on, keep devices updated (patching means installing fixes for known security holes), and stay alert.

items.myth: Phishing, meaning fake messages that trick you into clicking or sharing details, always has bad spelling and grammar.
items.fact: Many fake messages now look clean and professional. Attackers use AI tools to write them perfectly, so good spelling proves nothing.
items.detail: Look at what the message asks instead. Is it unexpected? Does it create pressure to act fast? Is the sender address slightly off? Those clues are far more reliable than typos.

items.myth: Public Wi-Fi is fine if the website shows a padlock.
items.fact: The padlock only means the connection to that site is encrypted (scrambled). It does not make the Wi-Fi network trustworthy or the site honest.
items.detail: A fake hotspot named like the cafe's can sit between you and the internet, and scam sites can have padlocks too. On public Wi-Fi, use a VPN (a tool that creates a private, encrypted tunnel for your traffic) or your phone's hotspot for work.

items.myth: If my password is strong, I never need to change it, even after a data breach.
items.fact: A strong password that has leaked is no longer safe. If a service you use is breached, change that password straight away.
items.detail: A breach means attackers now hold your actual password, however strong it was. Change it, never reuse it elsewhere, and use a password manager (an app that creates and stores a unique password for every account).

items.myth: Reusing one good password everywhere is fine, because it is easy to remember and strong.
items.fact: One leak exposes every account that shares it. Attackers try stolen passwords on many other sites automatically.
items.detail: This is called credential stuffing. Use a different password for every account. A password manager remembers them all so you only need to remember one.

items.myth: Multi-factor authentication (MFA, a second proof of identity such as a phone prompt or code) makes me unhackable.
items.fact: MFA blocks most account attacks, but it is not magic. Attackers can trick people into approving prompts or reading out codes.
items.detail: Never approve a prompt you did not start, and never read out a code to a caller. If prompts keep arriving, someone has your password: deny them and report it.

items.myth: Only careless or untrained people fall for social engineering, which means tricking people instead of hacking machines.
items.fact: Well-made pressure tactics fool careful, experienced people too. Urgency and authority work on everyone.
items.detail: Attackers research their targets and pick a busy moment. The safe habit is not being smarter than the scammer. It is pausing and checking through a second, trusted channel.

items.myth: If I click something I should not have, reporting it will get me in trouble.
items.fact: Reporting quickly is what protects you and the company. Most organisations care far more about speed than blame.
items.detail: Early reports let IT cut off an attack before it spreads. Hiding a mistake lets it grow, and that is what causes real damage.

items.myth: If I am not sure something is harmful, it is not worth reporting.
items.fact: Being unsure is exactly when to report. A two-minute check from IT costs little; a missed attack can cost a lot.
items.detail: Your report may be the missing piece that shows others received the same message. Report first, let the experts decide.
